Hi Abhi,

Can you clarify what you intend for Vw?  It’s a red flag that you have Vw[,] <- M[1:n,1:n] followed by another set of declarations that appear to be duplicate declarations for the same parts of Vw.  If so, that is not allowed and if it is getting through the system it could cause a problem.  BUGS is a declarative language, so each line draws a node and edges in the model graph.  The same node cannot subsequently be re-declared.  Order of declarations does not matter. 

I haven’t checked the math on whether those should be equivalent models, but purely in terms of the code, I think the placement of sigma should be ok either way.

A couple of suggestions for mixing:

The block sampler that would be sampling w[] can sometimes struggle in its adaptation in many dimensions.  You could try adding univariate random walk samplers to each element of w[].

That pattern of (poor) mixing for a standard deviation is not uncommon.  One simple trick that can help is to include a sampler that operates on a log scale.  Simply add a univariate random walk with “log = TRUE” in the control list.  You can do this in addition to the default random walk sampler that is already assigned to sigma, or you can remove that one to reduce the computation time if it really isn’t helping.

Perry

The qualitative appearance of the mixing of the sigmas does not look wildly different to me.  The top one gets entrained near zero for some of the later iterations.  But is that a truly different mixing regime or just a different stochastic realization?

One way you could check would be to set the inits and use set.seed from R to set the random number seed.  Then you could look at the samplers (mcmcConf$printSamplers()) to make sure that the slight change in how the model is written has not changed the order of the samplers (which could validly happen).  Assuming the samplers are in the same order (and you could reorder them if needed with mcmcConf$setSamplers) you could run each for a short number of iterations and see if they do exactly the same thing, starting from the same inits and the same seed.  Of course there may be numerical rounding differences in the two models but for a short number of iterations that doesn’t seem likely to lead to different MCMC results.  Is that the kind of diagnostic you are looking for?  If something is wrong, I think that would help us pin it down.

Perry

Hi, 

I am running a multivariate normal model with autoregressive covariance structure and found widely different results based on how I specified the covariance matrix. Please see the data and code below. The only difference between the two models is that the marginal variance sigma^2 is specified once before the cholesky and once after the cholesky of the correlation matrix. 
One of the versions (model 1) did not converge even though I ran it for a million iterations (the dataset only has 100 observations). I'm attaching the trace plots for two of the variables based on 10000 iterations. Any insight on this will be very helpful. 

Thanks,
Abhi

##### model1 ####
onedagarCode1 <- nimbleCode({
    
    M[,] <- nimbledagarone(udnei[],dni[],cni[],rho,n)
    Vw[,] <- M[1:n,1:n]
    for(i in 1:n){
        Vw[i,1:n]<-M[i,1:n]/(sqrt(M[n+1,i])*sigma)    ### only difference with model 2
    }
    G[,] <- chol(inverse(t(Vw[,])%*%Vw[,]))
    
    w[] ~ dmnorm(muw[], cholesky=G[,], prec_param=0)
    Vy[,] <- tau*id[,]
    mu[] <- X[,]%*%beta[]+w[]
    y[] ~ dmnorm(mu[], cholesky=Vy[,], prec_param=0)
    beta[] ~ dmnorm(mubeta[],cholesky=Cbeta[,], prec_param=0)
    sigma ~ dunif(0, 100)
    tau ~ dunif(0, 10)
    rho ~dunif(0,1)
})

##### model2 ####
onedagarCode2 <- nimbleCode({
    
    M[,] <- nimbledagarone(udnei[],dni[],cni[],rho,n)
    Vw[,] <- M[1:n,1:n]
    for(i in 1:n){
        Vw[i,1:n]<-M[i,1:n]/(sqrt(M[n+1,i]))
    }
    G[,] <- sigma*chol(inverse(t(Vw[,])%*%Vw[,])) ### only difference with model 1
    
    w[] ~ dmnorm(muw[], cholesky=G[,], prec_param=0)
    Vy[,] <- tau*id[,]
    mu[] <- X[,]%*%beta[]+w[]
    y[] ~ dmnorm(mu[], cholesky=Vy[,], prec_param=0)
    beta[] ~ dmnorm(mubeta[],cholesky=Cbeta[,], prec_param=0)
    sigma ~ dunif(0, 100)
    tau ~ dunif(0, 10)
    rho ~dunif(0,1)
})

#### common function used by both models ####
nimbledagarone=nimbleFunction(run=function(udnei=double(1),dni=double(1),cni=double(1),rho=double(0),n=double(0)){
    returnType(double(2))
    V <-matrix(0,n+1,n)
    for(i in 1:n) V[i,i]<-1
    for(i in 2:n){
        V[n+1,i] <- (1-rho^2)/(1+(dni[i-1]-1)*rho^2)
        for(j in 1:dni[i-1]){
            ind<- udnei[cni[i-1]-dni[i-1]+j]
            V[i,ind]<- -rho/(1+(dni[i-1]-1)*rho^2)
        }            
    }
    V[n+1,1]<-1
    return(V)
})

The qualitative appearance of the mixing of the sigmas does not look wildly different to me.  The top one gets entrained near zero for some of the later iterations.  But is that a truly different mixing regime or just a different stochastic realization?

One way you could check would be to set the inits and use set.seed from R to set the random number seed.  Then you could look at the samplers (mcmcConf$printSamplers()) to make sure that the slight change in how the model is written has not changed the order of the samplers (which could validly happen).  Assuming the samplers are in the same order (and you could reorder them if needed with mcmcConf$setSamplers) you could run each for a short number of iterations and see if they do exactly the same thing, starting from the same inits and the same seed.  Of course there may be numerical rounding differences in the two models but for a short number of iterations that doesn’t seem likely to lead to different MCMC results.  Is that the kind of diagnostic you are looking for?  If something is wrong, I think that would help us pin it down.

Perry

Hi Abhi,

Can you clarify what you intend for Vw?  It’s a red flag that you have Vw[,] <- M[1:n,1:n] followed by another set of declarations that appear to be duplicate declarations for the same parts of Vw.  If so, that is not allowed and if it is getting through the system it could cause a problem.  BUGS is a declarative language, so each line draws a node and edges in the model graph.  The same node cannot subsequently be re-declared.  Order of declarations does not matter. 

I haven’t checked the math on whether those should be equivalent models, but purely in terms of the code, I think the placement of sigma should be ok either way.

A couple of suggestions for mixing:

The block sampler that would be sampling w[] can sometimes struggle in its adaptation in many dimensions.  You could try adding univariate random walk samplers to each element of w[].

That pattern of (poor) mixing for a standard deviation is not uncommon.  One simple trick that can help is to include a sampler that operates on a log scale.  Simply add a univariate random walk with “log = TRUE” in the control list.  You can do this in addition to the default random walk sampler that is already assigned to sigma, or you can remove that one to reduce the computation time if it really isn’t helping.

Perry

Hi Abhi,

Can you clarify what you intend for Vw?  It’s a red flag that you have Vw[,] <- M[1:n,1:n] followed by another set of declarations that appear to be duplicate declarations for the same parts of Vw.  If so, that is not allowed and if it is getting through the system it could cause a problem.  BUGS is a declarative language, so each line draws a node and edges in the model graph.  The same node cannot subsequently be re-declared.  Order of declarations does not matter. 

I haven’t checked the math on whether those should be equivalent models, but purely in terms of the code, I think the placement of sigma should be ok either way.

A couple of suggestions for mixing:

The block sampler that would be sampling w[] can sometimes struggle in its adaptation in many dimensions.  You could try adding univariate random walk samplers to each element of w[].

That pattern of (poor) mixing for a standard deviation is not uncommon.  One simple trick that can help is to include a sampler that operates on a log scale.  Simply add a univariate random walk with “log = TRUE” in the control list.  You can do this in addition to the default random walk sampler that is already assigned to sigma, or you can remove that one to reduce the computation time if it really isn’t helping.

Perry

A couple of suggestions for mixing:

The block sampler that would be sampling w[] can sometimes struggle in its adaptation in many dimensions.  You could try adding univariate random walk samplers to each element of w[].

That pattern of (poor) mixing for a standard deviation is not uncommon.  One simple trick that can help is to include a sampler that operates on a log scale.  Simply add a univariate random walk with “log = TRUE” in the control list.  You can do this in addition to the default random walk sampler that is already assigned to sigma, or you can remove that one to reduce the computation time if it really isn’t helping.

Perry

Hi Abhirup, here's what is happening.

In the 6th iteration, a negative sigma is proposed. In model 1, this
produces a positive valued G, and the proposal is rejected because of the
-Inf log probability for sigma. In model 2, this produces a negative valued
G, and the proposal is rejected but based on a -Inf log probability for
sigma and an NaN log probability for w. Because of the NaN, there is a
slightly different set of calculations done, and the result is a shift by
one value in what random numbers are used subsequently in the MCMCs for the
two models. So then you get different stochastic realizations from the
posterior.

I agree with Perry that I don't see the two chains as really differing so
it's not the case that one is the 'correct' one to use. Both show poor
mixing and model 1 seems to get stuck, but if you run model 2 longer, I
suspect it would get similarly stuck at times.

If you use the 'log' option for the sigma parameter RW sampler (or the
'reflective' option), you shouldn't see this occur, because negative sigma
values won't ever be proposed. But that is just tidying up a numerical
anomaly, not changing the substance of the issue, which is the slow mixing.

For future reference for anyone reading this, I diagnosed this by running
the _uncompiled_ version of the MCMC, using debug(onedagarMCMC1$run) function
and stepping through the MCMC code.

-Chris

Hi Abhi,

Can you clarify what you intend for Vw?  It’s a red flag that you have Vw[,] <- M[1:n,1:n] followed by another set of declarations that appear to be duplicate declarations for the same parts of Vw.  If so, that is not allowed and if it is getting through the system it could cause a problem.  BUGS is a declarative language, so each line draws a node and edges in the model graph.  The same node cannot subsequently be re-declared.  Order of declarations does not matter. 

I haven’t checked the math on whether those should be equivalent models, but purely in terms of the code, I think the placement of sigma should be ok either way.

A couple of suggestions for mixing:

The block sampler that would be sampling w[] can sometimes struggle in its adaptation in many dimensions.  You could try adding univariate random walk samplers to each element of w[].

That pattern of (poor) mixing for a standard deviation is not uncommon.  One simple trick that can help is to include a sampler that operates on a log scale.  Simply add a univariate random walk with “log = TRUE” in the control list.  You can do this in addition to the default random walk sampler that is already assigned to sigma, or you can remove that one to reduce the computation time if it really isn’t helping.

Perry

Hi Abhirup, here's what is happening.

In the 6th iteration, a negative sigma is proposed. In model 1, this
produces a positive valued G, and the proposal is rejected because of the
-Inf log probability for sigma. In model 2, this produces a negative valued
G, and the proposal is rejected but based on a -Inf log probability for
sigma and an NaN log probability for w. Because of the NaN, there is a
slightly different set of calculations done, and the result is a shift by
one value in what random numbers are used subsequently in the MCMCs for the
two models. So then you get different stochastic realizations from the
posterior.

I agree with Perry that I don't see the two chains as really differing so
it's not the case that one is the 'correct' one to use. Both show poor
mixing and model 1 seems to get stuck, but if you run model 2 longer, I
suspect it would get similarly stuck at times.

If you use the 'log' option for the sigma parameter RW sampler (or the
'reflective' option), you shouldn't see this occur, because negative sigma
values won't ever be proposed. But that is just tidying up a numerical
anomaly, not changing the substance of the issue, which is the slow mixing.

For future reference for anyone reading this, I diagnosed this by running
the _uncompiled_ version of the MCMC, using debug(onedagarMCMC1$run) function
and stepping through the MCMC code.

-Chris

Can you clarify what you intend for Vw?  It’s a red flag that you have Vw[,] <- M[1:n,1:n] followed by another set of declarations that appear to be duplicate declarations for the same parts of Vw.  If so, that is not allowed and if it is getting through the system it could cause a problem.  BUGS is a declarative language, so each line draws a node and edges in the model graph.  The same node cannot subsequently be re-declared.  Order of declarations does not matter. 

I haven’t checked the math on whether those should be equivalent models, but purely in terms of the code, I think the placement of sigma should be ok either way.

A couple of suggestions for mixing:

The block sampler that would be sampling w[] can sometimes struggle in its adaptation in many dimensions.  You could try adding univariate random walk samplers to each element of w[].

That pattern of (poor) mixing for a standard deviation is not uncommon.  One simple trick that can help is to include a sampler that operates on a log scale.  Simply add a univariate random walk with “log = TRUE” in the control list.  You can do this in addition to the default random walk sampler that is already assigned to sigma, or you can remove that one to reduce the computation time if it really isn’t helping.

Perry
